title: How to keep AI product photos from getting flagged or rejected by marketplaces
summary: Most marketplaces allow AI product photos. They reject images that misrepresent the product, miss image specs or skip AI disclosure. How to stay compliant.
body_markdown:
*Marketplaces flag a product image when it stops matching the real product, misses a technical spec, or skips a required disclosure. The pixels being AI-made is fine on its own. Accuracy is the fix: start from a real product shot, hold color, proportion, and label text true to what ships, meet each channel's spec, and disclose AI where the rules require it. Do that and marketplaces have no reason to reject your photos, at one image or a million.*


---


A flagged listing stops earning the moment it is suppressed, and the damage compounds from there. A suppressed main image drops your listing out of search and buy-box eligibility, so traffic you already paid for lands on a dead page. An image that looks better than the product ships returns and refund claims, which drag your account health metrics down. Enough policy hits, and the marketplace restricts or suspends the account you built your revenue on.


For a seller with a handful of stock keeping units (SKUs), that is a bad week. For an enterprise team running thousands of listings across Amazon, Walmart, Etsy, eBay, and social commerce, one bad rule applied at scale can suppress a whole category overnight.


This article covers why AI product photos actually get rejected, the workflow that keeps them compliant, and what to look for in a tool if you need to run that workflow across a full catalog.


## Table of contents


## Are AI product images allowed on marketplaces?


Yes. Most major marketplaces allow AI-generated and AI-edited product images.


The confusion comes from treating "is AI allowed" as a single yes/no question when it's actually two separate ones:


-


**Permission:** Permission determines whether a specific image type is allowed. For example,[Etsy](https://www.etsy.com/legal/policy/listing-image-requirements/253962679005) requires original photos for listings that showcase the actual finished product but allows computer-generated mockups for additional listing images to showcase customization options.


-


**Disclosure:** Disclosure determines whether you're required to tell buyers that AI was involved in creating it. Some platforms might not care that you used AI to clean up the background, but will require a label if you used AI to generate a model wearing the product. Others draw the line differently, treating any AI involvement as disclosable regardless of how minor. For example,[Walmart](https://marketplacelearn.walmart.com/guides/Item%20setup/Item%20content,%20imagery,%20and%20media/Product-detail-page:-Image-guidelines-&-requirements) allows AI-generated images without disclosure, as long as they're truthful, accurate, and not misleading.


With a permission failure, the issue is the image's presence itself. The platform doesn't allow that type of AI image at all, so swapping in a compliant photo or removing the AI-generated element is the only fix.


A disclosure failure means the image is fine as-is, but you didn't tell anyone how it was made. Instead of adding a new photo, creating a label or metadata tag would be enough to bring it into compliance.

Not every marketplace's detection is equally reliable, and false positives aren't unique to any one platform. The goal is to make an image accurate enough that no marketplace has grounds to reject it and formatted precisely enough that it clears every technical spec on the first upload.


Once that's handled, the rest is easy by comparison: disclosure is a label or a metadata tag, and a false-positive flag is a quick appeal.


## What AI tends to get wrong in product photography


General-purpose image models are built to make a picture look good. A product image has a harder job: it has to look good and stay true to the item that ships. The errors below are where those two goals pull apart. They're also the ones marketplaces and buyers catch.


-


**Color drift.** A navy jacket comes out royal blue, or a beige sofa turns grey under new lighting. It looks minor on screen, but it's a common reason buyers return an item as "not as described."


-


**Garbled label and packaging text.** AI often redraws text instead of keeping it, so ingredient lists, sizes and brand names come out misspelled, blurred or invented. On regulated products like food, cosmetics and supplements, wrong on-pack text is a compliance problem, not just a cosmetic one.


-


**Distorted logos.** Logos get warped, simplified or swapped for something close but wrong. That can read as counterfeit, which is one of the fastest ways to get a listing pulled.


-


**Wrong proportions and scale.** A bag looks bigger than it is, a bottle gets taller, or the product looks the wrong size next to the props.


-


**Added or missing parts.** Extra buttons, a second strap, a missing handle, a zip that goes nowhere. AI fills gaps with what it thinks should be there.


-


**Changed materials and finishes.** Matte turns glossy, brushed metal turns chrome, a knit loses its texture. Buyers notice the moment they open the box.


-


**Broken patterns.** Stripes that bend, checks that don't line up at the seams, or a print that repeats wrongly across the garment.


-


**Props that look included.** A generated scene adds a strap, a stand or a matching accessory that doesn't come with the product. Buyers expect to receive what they see.


-


**Physics that don't add up.** Products floating above the surface, shadows falling the wrong way, reflections that don't match the scene. These make an image look fake even when the product itself is accurate.


-


**Messy cutout edges.** Halos, leftover background, or clipped edges around hair, fur, glass and fine details. Marketplaces that require a pure white background will flag these.


**Edits that rebuild the product carry the most risk.**


-


**Ghost mannequin** can leave a collar the wrong shape or an inside label missing.


-


**Flat lay** can change how a garment hangs or how long it looks.


-


**Virtual models** can misrepresent fit, and generated hands and bodies can still come out wrong.


[Most of these errors](https://www.photoroom.com/blog/how-to-fix-inaccurate-ai-product-images) are hard to spot at thumbnail size, and they slip through when someone is reviewing thousands of images. That's why the tool matters. A general image model can't tell that a logo changed or that a label now reads differently. A tool trained on product photography, with[quality checks built in](https://www.photoroom.com/enterprise/visual-qa) , is designed to catch these errors. It compares each output with the source, flags drift before anything is published, and sends only the doubtful images to a person for manual review.

## The compliance-safe AI workflow, step by step


Most rejections trace back to an image that no longer matches what ships. Close that gap and the rest usually falls into place.


Each step says what has to happen, then how it works when you're processing thousands of images. Get the steps right on one image, then run the same logic across your catalog.


1.


**Start from a real product shot.**


-


*What to do:* Use a photo of the actual unit as your source, so the AI builds on the real item instead of inventing one.


-


*At scale:* Pull source images straight from your product catalog or asset library. Where you have several angles (front, side, label close-up), pass them all in. The more references the AI has, the less it guesses.


2.


**Change how the product is shown, never what it is.**


-


*What to do:* Background swaps, ghost mannequin, flat lay and relighting all change how a product is presented. That's fine. What can't change is anything the buyer relies on: color, pattern, proportions, material, logos and label text.


-


*At scale:* Sort your edits by how much of the product they touch. A background swap can leave the product pixels untouched. Edits that rebuild part of the product, like removing a mannequin or reshaping a garment for flat lay, need a stricter check in step 4.


3.


**Meet each channel's spec.**


-


*What to do:* Match each marketplace's background, aspect ratio and minimum resolution.


-


*At scale:* Define each channel's spec once as an output setting. Every image then comes out in every required format, with no per-image editing.


4.


**Check the output against the source.**


-


*What to do:* Open the output at 100% next to the original photo. Check color, material, proportions and every character of on-pack text against the source image and your product data (official color names, dimensions, label copy). If anything differs, regenerate before you publish.


-


*At scale:* Run automated checks against the source on every image, such as color matching and reading label text. Apply the strictest checks to edits that rebuild the product, such as ghost mannequin and flat lay, since that's where drift is most likely. Send failures and a sample of passes to a person for review.


5.


**Disclose where required.**


-


*What to do:* Add the AI disclosure for any channel that asks for it.


-


*At scale:* Set disclosure per channel in your listing feed, and keep provenance metadata (the record of how the image was made) attached through export.


The steps stay the same at any volume. What changes is who does them: at catalog scale, steps 1–3 and 5 run in the pipeline, and step 4 becomes an automated check with people reviewing the exceptions. The next section covers what to look for in a tool that supports that.

## Best practices to keep AI images from getting flagged


The workflow gets each image right before it's published. These practices keep your listings compliant once they're live.


-


**Keep the source photo for every image.** If a listing is flagged, the original is your proof that the product is real and the image matches it. It's the fastest way to win an appeal on a false positive.


-


**Test a small batch before rolling out to a new channel.** Upload a few dozen images first, and scale only once they clear.


-


**Recheck channel rules regularly.** Marketplaces update image specs and AI disclosure rules. A setting that was compliant last year can get you flagged today.


-


**Track flags by channel and edit type.** If rejections cluster on one marketplace or one edit, like ghost mannequin, fix the rule behind them, not each image.


-


**Audit live listings, not just new ones.** Spot-check a sample of published images against their sources, especially after a model or workflow change.


Building these into your listing process now saves you from flagged listings, takedowns and lost sales later.


## Accurate images clear at any volume


Marketplaces don't reject AI. They reject images that misrepresent the product. Keep every image true to what ships, matched to each channel's spec and disclosed where required, and there's nothing left to flag.
